solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Barrow, very noisy, that's not got wheeled out

indicators.note: the long word is said not to have something, so that piece is taken away from it

parts.note: a very noisy crowd or din is tumultuous

indicators.note: something wheeled round turns about, so the word out is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone describes a loud wheelbarrow that has not been brought outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrow' suggests a wheelbarrow, matching 'wheeled', but it is the burial mound. The removed letters are TUO, out turned round by 'wheeled'.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow in archaeology is an ancient earth mound raised over a grave, the same thing as this Latin-derived word.

clue.text: Labour maintaining posh empty room causes unrest

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so the labour word holds the other letters

parts.note: toil is hard labour
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

indicators.note: empty leaves only the outer letters of the word room

explanation.surface: The Labour Party keeping a smart vacant room provokes discontent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party but is plain hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: Turmoil is a state of great disturbance and confusion, which is what unrest describes.

clue.text: Low bar spans Northern Line

indicators.note: the lowing word stretches across the abbreviation, holding it

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
a rail is a bar, as in a towel rail

explanation.surface: A low barrier stretches across the London Underground's Northern Line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern Line' reads as one London Tube line; it splits into N and the definition. 'Low' is the cow's noise, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A monorail is a railway running on a single track, so it is a kind of railway line.

clue.text: Supplier of narrow light dinghy

definitions.meaning: a device producing a narrow, intense beam of light
a popular one-person racing sailing dinghy class

explanation.surface: A small sailing boat fitted with a lamp giving a slim beam.
explanation.definitionFit: The device emits a tight coherent beam, and the same name belongs to a widely raced single-handed sailboat.

clue.text: West Coast city teams caught tailing present carrier

indicators.note: tailing means following behind, so the teams piece comes after

parts.note: Santa Claus carries presents at Christmas

indicators.note: caught as in heard, so the word for teams is taken by its sound

parts.note: crews are teams, as of rowers or workers

explanation.surface: A US city's sports sides are seen following Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like a cricket C but means heard, so CREWS becomes CRUZ.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Cruz is a city on the Pacific coast of California, south of San Francisco.

clue.text: Trooper occupying the back makes up crew

indicators.note: the whole assembly is then read backwards
the soldier takes up residence inside the word the

parts.note: GI is the usual crossword soldier, an American trooper

explanation.surface: A soldier sitting in the rear seat completes a team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The back' reads as a seat at the rear, but 'back' reverses the whole assembly, THGIE, not just THE.
explanation.definitionFit: In rowing an eight is a racing boat with eight oarsmen, so the word names the crew itself.

clue.text: Bogus bunch of bankers at Zurich

indicators.note: a bunch drawn out from the middle of the words, letters running consecutively

explanation.surface: Some Swiss bankers in Zurich are fraudulent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunch of' seems to count bankers but signals a run of letters taken from the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz describes an inferior imitation or substitute, so it is fake or bogus.

clue.text: Poor coaching's put off ace — they may be in the soup

definitions.text: they may be in the soup

indicators.note: poor means badly made, so the letters of coaching are rearranged
put off means removed, so one letter is taken out of the pool before rearranging

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: Bad coaching has deterred a top player, leaving the team in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: COACHING minus A gives the letters to rearrange. 'In the soup' sounds like 'in trouble', but gnocchi are dumplings often served in soup.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnocchi are small Italian dumplings, and dumplings are often served in a broth.

clue.text: The way things are going, start regularly then finish

indicators.note: taking every other letter of the word start, the even ones

parts.note: the end is the finish

explanation.surface: Advice to begin steadily, then wrap up, describing how matters develop.
explanation.definitionFit: A trend is a general direction in which something is developing or changing.

clue.text: Church Mass arranged in heart of Kent castle for one

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the middle letters
the middle letters of the word Kent
the letters of mass are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A church service is held inside a fortress in the English county of Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' turns the letters into SSMA. 'Castle' looks like a fortress, fitting Kent, but is the chess rook.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the castle, or rook, is one of the pieces, so it is an example of this.

clue.text: Woman's old name for tall winger

parts.note: her is the possessive pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A woman's former name is given to a tall person on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a football player; here it is a bird with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-legged wading bird stands tall and flies, so a tall winger is a playful description of it.

clue.text: Oddly, Spain doesn't fancy the Rock

indicators.note: taking the odd-numbered letters of the word Spain
fancy as an adjective means elaborate or reworked, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Spain, strangely, does not care for Gibraltar.
explanation.walkthrough: SAN from Spain's odd letters, then DSTONE from rearranging DOESNT. 'The Rock' looks like Gibraltar, Spain's old grievance, but it is any rock of that kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock of compressed sand grains, so it is an example of rock.

clue.text: United brought in successful player who cleans up?

indicators.note: the abbreviation is taken inside the player word

parts.note: a scorer is a player who gets goals or points
U is the standard abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: A football club signs a goal-getter who will tidy up the league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who cleans up?' sounds like a dominant player; the question mark marks the definition as playful, since a scourer is a pad, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourer is a scrubbing pad used to clean pots, so it is what does the cleaning up.

clue.text: Colonist, a hero, bringing remedy?

parts.note: an ant lives in a colony
El Cid was the Spanish national hero

explanation.surface: A settler and a champion arrive with a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonist' suggests a settler, but it is an insect living in a colony.
explanation.definitionFit: An antacid neutralises stomach acid, a remedy for indigestion; the question mark marks it as one example.

clue.text: Factory I came across dealing with small measure

parts.note: a mill is a factory, as in a cotton mill
to meet is to come across, past tense met
re means concerning or about

explanation.surface: Someone reports encountering a factory while handling a tiny quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre, a very small unit of length.

clue.text: Heather collects a couple of notes for obscure topics

indicators.note: the heather word gathers the notes inside it

parts.note: Erica is the botanical genus of heather
so and te are two notes of the sol-fa scale, side by side

explanation.surface: A woman called Heather gathers a few written messages about arcane subjects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name but is the plant. The notes go after ERICA's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoterica are things understood only by a small specialised circle, so they are obscure matters.

clue.text: Shame city centre's controlled by party extremists

indicators.note: being controlled means held in, so the middle sits inside the other letters
the outermost letters of the word party
the middle letters of the word city are taken

explanation.surface: A disgrace: the city centre is run by party radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremists' looks political but means the end letters P and Y; IT goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: "It's a shame" and "it's a pity" are interchangeable expressions of regret.

clue.text: One from Glasgow hosts peer, good runner

indicators.note: the Scottish word holds the peer inside it

parts.note: yin is Scots for one
an earl is a peer of the realm

explanation.surface: A Glaswegian welcomes a nobleman who is a fine athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good runner' reads as one phrase, but 'good' gives G and 'runner' is a racehorse.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearling is a horse in its second year, often sold as a potential racehorse, a runner in races.

clue.text: Gritty Greek circular lacking a name

indicators.note: without, so one letter is taken out of the ring word

parts.note: annular means ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A tough Greek leaflet arrives without an addressee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular' looks like a leaflet but is the adjective meaning ring-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: Granular means made of grains or particles, so it has a gritty texture.

clue.text: Curious revolutionary poet's last letters

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round, so the letters are read backwards
only the closing letters of the poet's name are kept, the front dropped

parts.note: Alfred Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate

explanation.surface: An inquisitive rebel reads a poet's final correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of TENNYSON, YSON, is turned round by 'revolutionary'. The clue does not say how many letters, so crossings help.
explanation.definitionFit: A curious person wants to know others' business, which is what a nosy one does.

clue.text: Extra clerical vestment picked up

indicators.note: picked up as in heard, so the vestment word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a surplice is a loose white linen garment worn by clergy and choristers

explanation.surface: A spare church garment is collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' looks like lifting the robe but means heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A surplus is an amount left over beyond what is needed, so it is extra.

clue.text: Last letters by medic are entirely about dairy product

indicators.note: the medic sits beside the letters, put first here

parts.note: MO is a medical officer
Z is the last letter of the alphabet, so two of them are last letters

indicators.note: about means turned round, so that word is read backwards

parts.note: all means entirely, as in all alone

explanation.surface: A doctor's final correspondence is all about milk products.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last letters' sounds like a final post but means Z twice; 'about' turns ALL into LLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozzarella is a soft Italian cheese, and cheese is made from milk.

clue.text: Crime nearly sorted out: Charlie's collared

indicators.note: being collared means held, so the letter is caught inside the rearranged word
sorted out means rearranged, so the letters of nearly are shuffled

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A crime is almost solved: the culprit Charlie has been arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collared' looks like a police arrest but puts C inside the shuffled NEARLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the legal name for theft, a criminal offence.

clue.text: Pondering briefly to absorb learner's fine material

indicators.note: the shortened word takes the letter into itself
cut short, so the last letter of the pondering word is dropped

parts.note: musing means pondering
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A thoughtful student takes in a fine piece of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Muslin is a lightweight, loosely woven cotton fabric.

clue.text: Rear enthusiast to cross river followed by another

indicators.note: the enthusiast word spans the river letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a nut is a fan, as in a fitness nut
another river, the Ure, which flows through Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A keen fan is asked to bring up children across two rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rear' looks like a noun (the back) but is the verb meaning bring up. 'Another' means a second river, here the Ure.
explanation.definitionFit: To rear children is to bring them up and look after them, the same as to nurture them.

clue.text: Moneybags lifts box office embargo

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting means reading upward, so the pieces are reversed

parts.note: a ban is an embargo

explanation.surface: A rich man raises a ban on the theatre box office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifts' sounds like ending the embargo but turns BOBAN upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A nabob is a very wealthy person, originally one who made a fortune in India, a moneybags.

clue.text: Common groups of species initially leaving

parts.note: a genus is a group of related species, plural genera

indicators.note: take the first letter of the word leaving

explanation.surface: Ordinary groups of species set out first.
explanation.definitionFit: Something general is widespread or common to all, as in general knowledge.

clue.text: Good wood flanks new grate

indicators.note: the two pieces sit either side of the abbreviation

parts.note: ash is a tree and its timber

explanation.surface: Fine timber surrounds a new fireplace grate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grate' looks like the fireplace noun but is the verb, as in grinding teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: To gnash the teeth is to grind them together, making a grating noise.

clue.text: Instrument from a laboratory upset first cosmonaut?

indicators.note: upset means overturned, so the two pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: Laika was the Soviet dog sent into orbit in 1957, the first animal to orbit Earth

explanation.surface: A tool from a lab disturbs the original space traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' turns A LAB into BALA. The question mark admits that Laika, a dog, is a stretch for a cosmonaut.
explanation.definitionFit: The balalaika is a Russian stringed folk instrument with a triangular body.

clue.text: Left a German claiming one reward for late night?

indicators.note: the outer letters take hold of the numeral, which goes within

parts.note: ein is German for a
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A departed German says he won a prize for staying up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like departed but gives L; 'a German' is the German article, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: After staying up late, staying in bed longer the next morning is the treat you allow yourself.

clue.text: Bowl bishop when batting

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
as can mean when, as in as I left
a cricket side batting is in

explanation.surface: A cricket instruction: a bishop is told to bowl while his side is batting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like the cricket verb but is the noun. In cricket the batting side is 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A basin is a round open dish for washing or mixing, much like a bowl.

clue.text: Burnt-out cases end up here, lost around hospital

indicators.note: the lost word goes round the abbreviation

parts.note: to go astray is to get lost
H is the standard abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Exhausted, burnt-out people end up wandering lost around a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burnt-out cases' sounds like exhausted people but means spent cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Finished cigarette ends, burnt down to the stub, are stubbed out in this dish.
